condition.label: nonspecific neck pain
condition.distinctions: Nonspecific neck pain excludes an identified structural/neurological cause. Cervical radicular pain, WAD, myelopathy and instability need separate assessment.

scope.population: Female office workers ages 25–53, neck pain over six months; excluded severe cervical structural/traumatic/postoperative disease and major competing conditions
scope.stage: Varies by source; acute/recent versus chronic and symptom irritability are explicitly retained. Unknown stage remains unknown.
scope.operativeStatus: Nonsurgical evidence predominates; no postoperative protocol approved or inferred.
scope.exclusions: Source-specific exclusions are applicability boundaries, not diagnosis-wide contraindications. Coexisting conditions and independently selected joint limits retain precedence.
scope.uncertainty:
- Ordinary training: activity and individualized progression compatible with assessed nonspecific neck pain; do not apply cervical-radicular, myelopathic, trauma or instability restrictions indiscriminately. No universal overhead press, shrug, neck extension/rotation or strength-training prohibition supported by retrieved evidence.
- Supportive candidates: neck motor-control/isometric endurance and scapular/upper-body strengthening, with exact execution/dose reviewed independently. A neck bridge is not interchangeable with low-load cervical isometrics.
- No validated numerical pain cutoff, load ceiling, ROM threshold or automatic progression rule extracted. Detailed adverse surveillance is a major gap.
- Newer 2025–2026 network analyses were located (Spine Journal S1529943025003444; PMC13401843; PMC13112673) but not used to infer personal “optimal” doses. Their rankings/study-level dose curves do not establish app starting loads.

sources.outcomes: Mueller et al., 2023 systematic review/meta-analysis. DOI 10.2519/jospt.2023.11820, PMID 37339388. Abstract and publisher results text. 68 trials chronic nonspecific neck pain; resistance, motor-control and mindfulness-based exercise versus controls/other exercises. Modality rankings do not prove alternatives dangerous or provide safe loads for individual users. Full protocol and harms extraction remains incomplete.

sources.population: Female office workers ages 25–53, neck pain over six months; excluded severe cervical structural/traumatic/postoperative disease and major competing conditions
sources.comparator: Neck strength versus endurance versus stretching/aerobic advice
sources.coInterventions: Upper-body/trunk exercises; multimodal institutional rehabilitation; four therapy sessions in active groups
sources.outcomes: Ylinen et al., 2003 RCT. DOI 10.1001/jama.289.19.2509, PMID 12759322, journal FT. FT. 180 female office workers with chronic nonspecific neck pain. Twelve-month isometric strength/dynamic endurance programs versus stretching/aerobic advice; supervised introductory rehabilitation then home practice encouraged three times weekly. Both active programs reduced pain/disability more; included upper-body dumbbell presses, rows and shrugs as part of package. Excluded major structural/radicular/traumatic/postoperative disease. Systematic adverse-event reporting not identified. Selected supervised population and mixed package prevent assuming every press/shrug is safe for every neck disorder; equally, findings undermine an evidence-free diagnosis-wide ban on all upper-body resistance work.
sources.uncertainty: Selected working women; multimodal package; no automatic transfer to cervical radicular pain or WAD
sources.harms: At 12 months 3% across groups felt pain worsened due to training. This self-report is not comprehensive systematic adverse-event surveillance.
sources.limitations: Selected working women; multimodal package; no automatic transfer to cervical radicular pain or WAD Trial exclusions delimit studied applicability; they do not establish general contraindications.

protocol.execution: Endurance: supine head lifts; strength: seated elastic-resisted neck effort forward/obliquely right/left/back; both upper-body dumbbell and bodyweight exercises
protocol.dose: Endurance 3×20 head lifts; strength 1×15 per direction, measured resistance target 80% maximal isometric strength. These are trial values, not personal starting loads
protocol.frequency: 12-day introduction with nine practice sessions; home encouraged three times weekly for a year
protocol.supervision: Specially trained PT; load/technique checked at baseline, 2, 6 and 12 months
protocol.progression: Strength resistance recalibrated from measured isometric testing; endurance load unchanged
protocol.stoppingRules: not reported as a validated symptom cutoff; every other introductory session half intensity to reduce excessive loading
